title: Help everywhere
hookLine: Guru Gobind Singh, be our help everywhere

lines: THE TENTH GURU WROTE THE STANZA.
cards: Here's a detail that's easy to miss when the Ardas goes by at full speed. Guru Gobind Singh wrote its opening stanza.
He names Guru Nanak, then each Guru after him, one by one, all the way to his own father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. And then he stops. Of course he doesn't name himself: it's his poem.

But Sikhs who pray the Ardas today hear the tenth Guru's name right after the ninth, in exactly the same words. Someone added it, and the words they chose had been sitting at the end of the stanza all along.

teach.b: The stanza ends: sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, be our help in every place. Sabh is all. Thaaeen is places.
Sahaai, an old friend by now, is the helper. So the Var's opening asks every Guru it has named to be our help, everywhere.
Then the Ardas, as Sikhs pray it, goes on: dasvaan paatshaah, sri guru gobind singh sahib ji, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai. The tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, be our help in every place.

teach.h: THE POEM'S LINE, GIVEN TO THE POET.
teach.b: The community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet.
The one who left himself out is written back in. And it fits him. He became Guru as a boy, after his father's execution.
He wrote poetry and, tradition says, kept a court of poets at Anandpur. He founded the Khalsa. He fought battles, lost his sons, and lived through siege, flight and grief.

And before his death, Sikh tradition says, he ended the line of human Gurus: from then on the Guru would be the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa community. So this isn't a vague wish.

It's asked of someone remembered in the court and on the battlefield, in the forest and in grief. Sikhs ask him to be present wherever they go: the job interview, the hospital waiting room, the long drive home.
And the prayer doesn't ask for help in some places.

how: After remembering the first nine Gurus in Guru Gobind Singh's own stanza, the Ardas names the tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, and asks him to be the community's help in every place.

o: help given only inside a gurdwara's walls
a promise that nothing hard will happen
asking the Guru for help in every place, not some

p: where he kept a court of poets

s: Guru Gobind Singh named himself in the stanza he wrote
he stopped at his father; the Ardas adds his name with the same words.
sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai asks for help in every place
not some places: all of them.
Sikh tradition says the tenth Guru passed the Guruship to the scripture
before his death, to the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa.

games.q: you're praying the Ardas. the stanza has named nine Gurus and ended: be our help in every place. what comes next?
o: the tenth master is named, with the same words: be our help in every place.
the names start again from Guru Nanak.
games.why: the community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet, Guru Gobind Singh.

practice: Think of the places you'll be this week, your desk, your car, a hard conversation, your own kitchen late at night, and pick the one where you feel most alone. Picture yourself there.
If you pray, ask in the Ardas's own words, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, and feel that it includes this place; if you don't, picture someone you trust standing beside you.

wordCard.voice: Help everywhere. Sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai: the last line of the tenth Guru's stanza, which the Ardas gives back to him.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sabh thaaeen, in every place; the refrain that closes the Ardas's opening stanza.

carryVoice: Your line: present in every place. That includes the one you pictured. See you tomorrow.
